Dendritic cells are the only cells that can do this. They have a variable expression of their MHC and CCR7 molecules depending on their location in the body. In normal tissue they express high levels of the PRR, but low levels of the CCR7, so are not easily detected by the immune system. However, if the body is breached, the dendritic cells will detect the PAMPs and be activated. This will cause them to upregulate their CCR7 expression, and so they can now be detected by the CCR7 expressing naive T cells in the lymph nodes. The dendritic cells will also upregulate their MHC expression, and so they can present the correct MHC/peptide complex to the T cell.

The correct answer is B :)  The reason for this is that the ECG shows signs of an inferior MI, which means that the occlusion is most likely in the inferior part of the heart.  The leads that deviate in an inferior MI are leads II, III and aVF.  This is because the heart is electrically silent within the myocardium so the excess electrical activity from the ventricles is conducted through the epicardium.  In an MI the excess electrical activity from the ventricles is silent within the myocardium so the excess electrical activity is conducted through the endocardium.  In an inferior MI the endocardium is closest to the surface of the body in the direction of the positive electrode of the ECG leads that deviate.  Therefore the ECG shows deviating waves in these leads.  This was covered in the case 12 lecture on cardiac arrest and acute MI.

The correct answer is C, a pulmonary shunt.  This is because the patient is not responding to oxygen therapy, which would be expected to improve oxygenation in all the other conditions.  A pulmonary shunt is where blood passes through the lungs without coming into contact with the alveoli, so this would cause a low PiO2 that would not respond to oxygen therapy.  A VQ mismatch is where there is ventilation of alveoli that are not perfused, or perfusion of alveoli that are not ventilated. This would cause a low PiO2 that would respond to oxygen therapy.  Diffusion impairment is where the diffusion capacity of the membrane is reduced, so the oxygenation deficit would be seen in exercise but not at rest.  Hypoventilation would cause a high PaCO2 and a low PaO2, both of which would respond to oxygen therapy.
